newsitem.title: USA: U.S. official upbeat on consumer spending outlook.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official upbeat on consumer spending outlook.

text.p: A senior Clinton administration official voiced optimism on Tuesday about the outlook for consumer spending in 1997, even if the stock market runs into some troubles this year.

"The consumer is entering 1997 with ... confidence, optimism and income amd they should continue to stay in the stores through this year," U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television.
The Commerce Department reported earlier that retail sales rose 0.6 percent in December.
Ehrlich said he was not overly concerned about the high levels of consumer debt and argued that the rise in debt looked like a "rational portfolio choice" given the steep rise in asset prices.
"I don't think the household sector would react in a major way to a minor correction in equities market right now," he added.
Ehrlich declared that the U.S. economy overall was in "A+" shape, with the inflation picture "very, very positive".
The Labor Department reported earlier that consumer prices rose 0.3 percent in December, bringing the increase for the year as a whole to 3.3 percent.
"There are no meaningful signs of rising price pressures at the final stages of output," Ehrlich said, adding, "We look to be beyond the crest in agricultural prices."

He said rising oil prices were an "issue," with stocks fairly lean and Europe and North America hit by bad winter weather. "But," he added, "we're in a position now where we could imagine getting through the rest of this winter and into the spring without a further acceleration in energy prices."
Ehrlich acknowledged that wages have risen strongly over the last two months, but he argued they have not increased at a pace that would prove to be inflationary.

"I don't think we're out of that golden zone where real wages rise and yet not at a rate that productivity can't finance," he said. "We ought to be optimistic about the prospects for staying in that zone," he added.
One factor that seems to have helped contain inflation is the strength of the dollar, which rose to a nearly 30-month high against the German mark on Tuesday.

"The strength of the dollar has helped on the inflation picture," Ehrlich said. "And in turn the strength of the dollar has been caused in part by confidence in the U.S. economy, so in fact it's in something of a virtuous circle."
Asked about the major risks to the U.S. economy, Ehrlich cited energy prices and lacklustre growth in some of America's trading partners.
While growth in Canada and Mexico is picking up, western Europe and Japan are a concern, he said.
"We still need to be concerned about growth in western Europe, particularly as it approaches the Maastricht conditions," Ehrlich.
Under the Maastricht treaty, European countries that wish to participate in the start of monetary union in 1999 must meet stiff budget conditions this year.

"And," Ehrlich added, "we certainly need to be concerned about growth in Japan, where fiscal stimulus and monetary stimulus have both been tried and the economy remains in something of a flat position."
He advocated structural reforms in Japan that would open up the economy and promote growth.
